output.title: When demo theatre becomes a hidden workflow cost
output.body:
If you run a small business, demo theatre has a quiet cost: you can spend good time proving that something could work while the real workflow keeps waiting. That usually shows up as polished demos, POCs, or one more tool test that never reaches the repetitive work on your desk.

The real bill is not the demo itself. It is the time not spent on one recurring workflow with a measurable output. In a 1–10 person business, that often looks like repeated questions, manual data work, follow-ups, or invoice handling. If the work is not repeating, AI is probably not the right place to start. No shame in that; the machine can wait.

Bareni’s diagnostic is deliberately bounded. We look for one recurring workflow, check whether AI actually fits, and if it does, define a fixed-price pilot with clear measures. There is no mandatory roadmap gate in the middle. Timings and scope are intended, not guarantees. If someone wants strategy only, that is a separate conversation, not the default path.

We also keep scope discipline: no high-sensitivity medical, legal, or financial work; no bulk cold-email automation; no scan-heavy OCR-dependent jobs; and no request that depends on unsupported compliance or security claims. Those are current limits, not a claim that such work can never be automated.

A useful filter is simple: do you have one repeating workflow that plausibly takes about 5–10 hours a week, with an output you can measure and a human still approving the risky part? If not, demo theatre is probably the wrong place to spend more time.
